extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; scientists and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to observe, describe, abstract, and form conceptions for induction in scientific inquiry — distinguishing perception from inference and selecting appropriate abstractions/hypotheses. Emphasizes comparison, measurement as inferential, and the tentative trial-and-error of finding useful conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and inference are intimately blended; what we are said to observe is usually a compound result, of which one-tenth may be observation, and the remaining nine-tenths inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or reporting an observation, separate the raw sensations (e.g., 'I hear a sound', 'I had a visual sensation of a colored surface') from the inferred causes or identifications (e.g., 'that sound is a man's voice', 'I saw my brother'). Examples: hearing a voice vs hearing a sound; seeing a brother vs having visual sensations commonly produced by that person. Treat as error any failure to discriminate these layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report sensations separately from inferred objects or causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation extends only to the sensations by which we recognize objects; propositions we make relate mostly to the objects themselves and therefore usually add inference to sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In descriptions and records, explicitly note the sensory datum distinct from the interpretation (mark diagnostics used, prior experience invoked). This reduces conflating perception with identification and makes later inductive reasoning more transparent. Anti-patterns: stating only the inferred object without recording the sensory basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that description necessarily asserts resemblances (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in a description, to be the statement of a resemblance, or resemblances; to describe is to assert a connection between the perceived particular and other things denoted or connoted by the terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that any verbal description imports classification — you are implicitly comparing the observed instance to a class. When describing, specify the criteria of resemblance or the class-membership you are asserting to avoid surreptitious assumptions. Example: saying 'I see something white' asserts resemblance to the class 'white things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat measurement as partly inferential/deductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Many so-called observations (e.g., measurements) are not immediate perceptions but conclusions from reasoning; measurement often involves auxiliary mathematical or logical premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using measurements as observational data, document the measuring procedure and the inferential steps (standards, units, calculations). Example: 'the animal is ten feet long' is a deduction using a two-foot rule plus arithmetic; note premises like calibrations and mathematical assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent instances to guard against inferential error
rubrics_metrics.description: Each particular proposition usually involves an inference from sensation to fact, and this inference may be erroneous in any one instance, but is unlikely to be erroneous in all if sufficient in number to eliminate chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer general propositions founded on many independent observations rather than relying on a single perceived instance. Emphasize replication and independent diagnostics to reduce the chance of systematic misinference.

rubrics_metrics.name: The logic of observation: discriminate perceptions/feelings from inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of observation consists solely in a correct discrimination between that, in a result of observation, which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical purposes, reduce observational claims to (a) sensations or states of consciousness (outer/inner feelings) and (b) any inferences drawn from them; treat the former as the closest available datum. Defer metaphysical debates about perception of anything beyond consciousness when doing methodological work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat colligation/hypothesis as subsidiary to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation of facts by means of hypotheses (conceptions) is not induction itself but a preliminary/subsidiary operation: finding in what circumstances observed instances agree prepares the material for genuine induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to group and highlight agreements among observed instances (Kepler's ellipse example), but evaluate hypotheses by subsequent inductive steps (checking unobserved cases). Avoid conflating the act of positing a unifying hypothesis with the inductive generalization that extrapolates to unobserved instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be clear and appropriate to the inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions, to be subservient to induction, must be 'clear' and 'appropriate' — appropriate meaning the conception corresponds to real agreements among phenomena relevant to the object of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming categories or concepts for induction, choose conceptions that capture the important agreements among phenomena for the target question. Example of failure: Aristotle's 'body moves toward its own place' was an inappropriate conception because it excluded many cases and included non-cases. Assess a conception by (a) whether it runs through all relevant cases and (b) whether it excludes irrelevant ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form conceptions by comparison and abstraction (often from the phenomena themselves)
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions are obtained by abstraction from individual things via comparison; many useful scientific conceptions are evolved from the very phenomena they are meant to collate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively compare instances to abstract candidate conceptions; expect that the right conception may emerge from the phenomena rather than pre-existing in the mind. Document the comparisons that produced the conception and be prepared to refine it as new cases are examined. Note exceptions where conception must be supplied from external knowledge (e.g., ellipse idea when the track is invisible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a provisional 'type' or standard for large comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing many objects, a type or standard object is an indispensable condition of comparison; we fix upon one object as our standard and compare others against it, forming abstractions by noticing recurring shared circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select representative standards consciously; when a candidate standard fails to capture a large class, restart with a different starting point. Keep track of which standard was used and why; refine or drop the conception if it fails to group further instances usefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a tentative, iterative approach to finding appropriate conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The right conception is found by a tentative process — trying one conception and then another, changing the starting point, and recomparing until a conception that captures the important agreements is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat categorization and hypothesis-formation as iterative: form a conception, test it against additional instances, drop or generalize it if it fails, and repeat. Record failures and the adjustments made (e.g., dropping some circumstances to obtain a more general conception).
